Philosophy, Free Will, and Data Analysis

Before we dive into our laptops today, I want to start with a bit of a philosophical question: What makes us different from Artificial Intelligence?

As AI gets more capable, it’s easy to wonder where we fit in. Some of you mentioned free will, or having a soul, or the ability to actually go out and experience the physical world rather than just ingesting training data. I’ll buy all of that. But I think one of the biggest things we have that AI lacks is desire.

We choose to do things because we want to, or because we care about the outcome. AI does not care. If you ask an AI to make a graph, it doesn’t intrinsically care if that graph looks terrible. It will just execute what it thinks you want based on its parameters. If you don’t care about making a good graph, you aren’t going to get one. It is entirely up to us to provide the intent, the direction, and the standards.

Today, our desire is to make a really nice, scientifically rigorous graph to extract a physical constant from messy data. We are going to use AI to help us write the code, but we are the ones driving the science.

You can download today’s combined dataset here: https://tinyurl.com/N2314-260923-combined-data.

Visualizing the Data: The Baby Steps

In a real research lab, you are rarely handed clean data with a known answer. You usually have a messy spreadsheet full of variables, and you have to decide what to plot, how to fit it, and how to extract a meaningful number. Today, we are testing our data analysis chops by trying to quantify g, the acceleration due to gravity. Yes, we already know what g is on Earth, but this is a fantastic sandbox to practice our quantitative methods.

Let’s fire up Google Colab. We have a CSV file containing data from various pendulums measured by different groups in our class. We have two different masses (5\text{ g} and 70\text{ g}) and various string lengths.

Our primary variables of interest are:

  • T: The oscillation period (in seconds).

  • L: The length of the pendulum (in meters).

I’m going to prompt our AI assistant to read the CSV file. I’ll tell it: "We have a CSV file with data acquired from various pendulums. Different masses (5g and 70g), measured by different groups (A, B, C, Emori). Please plot the oscillation period (T, 5th column) versus the square root of length (\sqrt{L}, 4th column in meters)."

Why the square root of length? Let’s look at the plot the AI generates first.

Notice how the data forms a relatively straight line? This is intentional. If we had plotted T directly against L, we would get a curve. By plotting against \sqrt{L}, we linearize the data. Let’s look at the physics to understand why.

Linearizing the Pendulum Equation

From introductory physics, we know the theoretical relationship between the period T and the length L of an ideal pendulum is:

\begin{equation} \tag{1} T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \end{equation}

where g is the gravitational acceleration. If we want to fit a straight line to our data, we need to map this physics equation onto the standard equation for a line:

\begin{equation} \tag{2} y = m \cdot x + b \end{equation}

Here, y is our vertical axis, x is our horizontal axis, m is the slope, and b is the vertical intercept. Let’s rearrange Equation 1 slightly to separate the constant terms from our variable L:

\begin{align} \tag{3} T &= \left( \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{g}} \right) \sqrt{L} + 0 \end{align}

By comparing Equation 2 and Equation 3, we can define our axes and parameters:

y = T
x =
m = =
b = 0

This tells us that if we plot T on the y-axis and \sqrt{L} on the x-axis, the slope of that line (m) contains our desired parameter, g. We can solve for g algebraically:

\begin{align} m &= \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{g}} \nonumber \\ \sqrt{g} &= \frac{2\pi}{m} \nonumber \\ g &= \left( \frac{2\pi}{m} \right)^2 \tag{4} \end{align}

Fitting the Data (and Managing Precision)

Now that we know the math, we need to instruct the AI to fit a line to our data. But we can’t just say "fit a line." We have to be specific.

Looking at Equation 3, the vertical intercept b is exactly zero. Physics dictates this: if a pendulum has zero length, it has zero period. It doesn’t make sense to have a non-zero time for a non-existent string. So, we must explicitly tell the AI to force the fit line through the origin (0,0).

Furthermore, I’m going to ask the AI to calculate g directly using our relationship, and—this is a big one—I’m going to tell it to limit the precision of g to one decimal place.

Why? Imagine the AI spits out g = 10.78256767 \text{ m/s}^2. If you hand that number to a boss who was a STEM major, they are going to judge you harshly. There is simply no way our highly scattered, hand-timed stopwatch data is precise down to the hundred-millionths of a decimal place. Claiming that level of precision actually undermines your credibility as a scientist. We will stick to one decimal place.

The AI followed instructions well. The line goes through the origin, and we get a quantified parameter of g = 10.8 \pm 0.5 \text{ m/s}^2.

Refining the Model: Handling Outliers

We could stop here, but looking at the graph, a few data points are pulling our trend line away from where the bulk of the data sits. In experimental science, if you have a known source of error or a clearly anomalous dataset, it is sometimes appropriate to exclude those outliers—provided you document exactly what you are doing and why.

Let’s ask the AI to color-code the data by group (A, B, C, Emori) and use different symbols for the 5\text{ g} and 70\text{ g} masses. When we do this, it becomes visually apparent that Group B’s data points are consistently off the main trend line.

I’ll prompt the AI to generate a new plot excluding Group B from the fit calculation.

By removing those specific outliers, our fit tightens up significantly. We now get g = 9.4 \pm 0.3 \text{ m/s}^2. This is slightly closer to the accepted value of 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2. (If we were to cherry-pick a few more of the highest-length outliers to remove, we’d land almost exactly on 9.8, though we have to be careful not to over-manipulate our data!).

The Point-by-Point Method (Using Excel)

Plotting and fitting is the most robust way to analyze large datasets, but what if we just wanted to calculate g directly for every single trial? We can do a point-by-point calculation.

Let’s take our base equation (Equation 1) and solve it explicitly for g:

\begin{align} T &= 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \nonumber \\ T^2 &= 4\pi^2 \left(\frac{L}{g}\right) \nonumber \\ g \cdot T^2 &= 4\pi^2 L \nonumber \\ g &= \frac{4\pi^2 L}{T^2} \tag{5} \end{align}

If we know L and T for a specific trial, we can plug them into Equation 5 to get g. Doing this 50 times on a pocket calculator would take 20 minutes. Doing it in Excel takes seconds.

We set up our spreadsheet with columns for Mass, Length (cm), Length (m), and Period (s). In a new column for g, we type our formula. In Excel syntax, 4\pi^2 is written as ‘4*PI()2‘. We divide that by the Period squared (‘E32‘) and multiply by the Length in meters (‘D3‘).

Once we hit enter, we get a value for that specific row. We can then drag that formula down to apply it to the entire dataset.

Because some groups didn’t measure the period for certain lengths, those cells are blank. Excel interprets a blank cell as a zero, and since we are dividing by T^2, we get a ‘#DIV/0!‘ error.

If we try to use the standard ‘=AVERAGE()‘ function on this column, Excel will panic because of those error cells. We could manually delete them, but in the age of AI, we can just ask for a better way. I asked Gemini how to average a column while ignoring errors, and it suggested the ‘AGGREGATE‘ function.

To get the average while ignoring errors, we use ‘=AGGREGATE(1, 6, F2:F57)‘. The ‘1‘ tells Excel to calculate an average, and the ‘6‘ tells it to ignore error values.

We also want the standard deviation to act as our error bar, showing how spread out our point-by-point calculations are. We use ‘=AGGREGATE(7, 6, F2:F57)‘, where ‘7‘ is the command for standard deviation.

After formatting the cells to a reasonable single decimal point of precision, we get an average g of roughly 11 \pm 4 \text{ m/s}^2.

This means we are fairly confident the true value lies somewhere between 7 \text{ m/s}^2 and 15 \text{ m/s}^2. Considering how crude our stopwatch experiments were, and how simplistic this point-by-point average is compared to a proper linear fit, capturing the true value (9.8) within our error bounds is a solid success.

Getting comfortable with these tools—whether it’s prompting Python scripts in Colab or using advanced functions in Excel—takes practice. Don’t feel bad if you wouldn’t have thought to use the ‘AGGREGATE‘ function on your own; I didn’t know it either until I asked the AI! Building this intuition is an incremental process, and you are all off to a great start.
